text: Lesson 20 drew a line: a timeout or a server error is often worth retrying, because the failure may be transient — the external system was briefly overloaded, and the same request might succeed moments later. But how you retry matters just as much as whether you retry. Get that part wrong, and the retry logic itself becomes the problem.

Retrying immediately, in a tight loop, is the worst option. If the external system is struggling because it's overloaded, a flood of immediate retries from every caller makes that overload worse, not better. A fixed interval — always exactly two seconds — is an improvement, but it still doesn't give a genuinely struggling system real room to recover.

The proven strategy is exponential backoff: each retry waits progressively longer than the one before it — one second, then two, then four, then eight — instead of a flat interval. This code starts a backoffMs variable at one second, executes the request, returns immediately on success, and on failure calls gs.sleep with the current backoff, then doubles it before looping again. gs.sleep is a real server-side API that pauses script execution for the given number of milliseconds. Doubling that delay on every failed attempt is what makes this exponential instead of fixed.

None of this is safe unless the operation being retried is idempotent — meaning running it twice produces the same end result as running it once. Here's the real danger: if a create-incident call actually succeeded on the external system's side but the response was lost before your script saw it, a blind retry creates a second, duplicate incident for the same alert. Idempotency is the property that prevents exactly that.

The real ServiceNow technique for this should look familiar — it's the same coalesce idea from this track's Transform Map lesson, applied in script. Before inserting, this code queries for an existing record by u_external_alert_id, the coalesce field. If one's found, it's a retry or a duplicate webhook, so the script updates that record instead of creating a new one. Only when no match exists does it insert. Run this once, or run it three times because the first two responses timed out — the end state is identical, exactly one incident record, which is what makes it safe to sit inside that retry loop.

Exponential backoff controls how aggressively you retry; idempotency controls what's safe to retry at all. Together they're what turns a risky retry loop into a reliable one. Next lesson turns to the other half of handling failure well: logging integration activity clearly enough that when something does fail, you can actually tell why, instead of staring at a bare 'error occurred' message.
